query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by interface‐mediated dislocation climb that is enhanced by the severe lattice distortions and short‐range order differences between the alternating FCC and BCC layers. These interfaces create localized coherency stresses that act as barriers to dislocation motion initially but eventually promote dislocation climb and accumulation, leading to an accelerated creep response relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating comprising alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers with inherent compositional complexity and lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Apply a constant stress (creep loading) over an extended duration under controlled temperatures (e.g., room temperature and ~500–600 °C) to the multilayer sample versus a homogeneous HEA of the same composition.
generation.conditions: Constant uniaxial loading (creep) tests performed at both room temperature and elevated temperature (~500–600 °C) with identical loading conditions, ensuring that the multilayer architecture (with nanoscale layer thickness) remains intact.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale interfaces between FCC and BCC layers where differences in lattice parameters, short-range order, and consequent coherency stresses locally modulate dislocation mobility.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading, dislocations initially pile up at the multilayer interfaces due to incoherency and lattice distortions; over time, stress concentrations at these barriers promote dislocation climb via lattice diffusion, leading to a progressive acceleration in plastic deformation (creep) compared to a homogeneous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an identical homogeneous HEA, the multilayer sample will exhibit an initially similar deformation rate that becomes increasingly accelerated over time. Observation of higher local dislocation densities at the interfaces and a marked increase in creep strain rate would support the hypothesis.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous high-entropy alloy with a comparable overall composition but lacking the nanoscale multilayer architecture (and hence fewer coherency-induced barriers).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies as long as the multilayer architecture is maintained (nanoscale layer thicknesses) and within temperature/stress regimes where diffusion-assisted dislocation climb is activated (e.g., moderate to elevated temperatures, below any phase transformation thresholds).
generation.uncertainty: The exact rate of creep acceleration and the quantitative contribution of dislocation climb versus other deformation mechanisms remain uncertain due to the complex interplay of lattice distortion, short-range order, and diffusion kinetics in HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with identical overall compositions: one set as FCC/BCC multilayers with controlled nanoscale layer thickness, and a second set as a homogeneous alloy without distinct layers. Conduct constant-load creep tests at room temperature and an elevated temperature (~500–600 °C) while periodically stopping the test to characterize the dislocation structures at the interfaces using TEM and EBSD.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves for both sample sets
Local dislocation density measurements at the multilayer interfaces and within the homogeneous sample
Analysis of interfacial coherence and evidence of dislocation climb (e.g., diffusion markers or void formation) via high-resolution microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer sample does not exhibit a significantly accelerated creep strain rate over time relative to the homogeneous sample or if no increased accumulation of dislocations at the interfaces is observed, then the hypothesis that interface-mediated dislocation climb governs the progressive plastic deformation is falsified.

System: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy (Co-free variant of the Cantor alloy). Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software with Embedded-atom method (EAM) potential; model size 108.3 Å × 108.3 Å × 180.5 Å (180,000 atoms); relaxation via heating to 1000 K and cooling to 300 K; tensile loading at temperatures of 10 K, 300 K, 600 K and strain rates of 10^8 s^-1, 10^9 s^-1, 10^10 s^-1 along <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> orientations..
